articles.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? Tools, resources, transports and auth, explained by someone who built a server
articles.excerpt: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities, mainly tools the m…
articles.body: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities, mainly tools the model can call, resources it can read, and prompts users can choose. An MCP client , inside an app such as Claude, ChatGPT or an IDE, connects to the server and offers those capabilities to the model. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 , carried over stdio for local servers or Streamable HTTP for remote ones, and remote servers use OAuth 2.1 for authorization. Before MCP, every AI app needed its own integration for every service; with MCP, one server works with any client that speaks the protocol.
articles.author: Ali Ahmed

articles.title: My Second iPhone Lives at Home. I Use It From Anywhere.
articles.excerpt: I have two phone numbers in two countries. For a long time that meant two phones: one in my pocket, one in a drawer or a bag, and the second one was always the wrong one. A bank sends its code to the…
articles.body: I have two phone numbers in two countries. For a long time that meant two phones: one in my pocket, one in a drawer or a bag, and the second one was always the wrong one. A bank sends its code to the old number. A messaging account is tied to it. Someone who only has that number calls while it is at the bottom of a backpack on silent. Moving the number somewhere else does not fix it. Call forwarding and virtual numbers keep the number, not the phone, and most of what I need from that phone is the apps on it: banking, WeChat, a government app, two-factor codes. Those apps know what device they live on. A new device or a foreign IP gets a verification wall, and sometimes a frozen account.

articles.title: Five of Five: Run It Again Before You Trust an Agent
articles.excerpt: Cross-post of Insights #18. Canonical: https://sheikhwasim.com/insights/five-of-five-run-it-again-before-you-trust-it/ The demo worked. So did the second try. The third one quietly sent a claim to the…
articles.body: Cross-post of Insights #18. Canonical: https://sheikhwasim.com/insights/five-of-five-run-it-again-before-you-trust-it/ The demo worked. So did the second try. The third one quietly sent a claim to the wrong queue. Most agent evaluations ask one question: can it do the task? Run it once, read the output, nod. That tells you the agent is capable. It does not tell you the agent is dependable, and production only cares about the second one. The fix is a simple habit I call Five of Five : before an agent ships, every test case runs several times, and a case only passes if every run passes. Quick use case Situation. An insurance operations team builds an intake agent.

articles.title: Keeping AI answers findable when you use ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini
articles.excerpt: A good AI answer is easy to get once. Finding it again two weeks later is the hard part. You use ChatGPT for one kind of task, Claude for another and Gemini for a third. Then one day you need that pri…
articles.body: A good AI answer is easy to get once. Finding it again two weeks later is the hard part. You use ChatGPT for one kind of task, Claude for another and Gemini for a third. Then one day you need that pricing table, that regex or that email draft you worked out last week. You remember the answer. You don't remember which AI gave it to you, let alone which chat. So you scroll, try a few keywords, and often just ask the question again. If that sounds familiar, the problem usually isn't search. It's that the answer lives in one of three separate histories, under a title you typed in a hurry. What each app gives you today Each assistant has its own way to group work. ChatGPT and Claude have Projects, and Gemini has its own workspace features. They help inside one app.

articles.title: Making a portfolio of open public-sector projects that keeps itself honest
articles.excerpt: I maintain ten open projects on data and AI for UK public services. The hard part isn't building them. It's keeping the list of them accurate: which exist, what state each is in, what licence it's und…
articles.body: I maintain ten open projects on data and AI for UK public services. The hard part isn't building them. It's keeping the list of them accurate: which exist, what state each is in, what licence it's under, and when it last changed. This post covers the routines that now do that work, and the one rule they all follow: they propose, and a person merges. A daily discovery routine compares my public repositories with the launchpad's project list. For a new repository, it drafts a card from what the repository says about itself, labels anything it can't know, and puts the draft on a branch for review. The profile README rebuilds itself from that list once a change is merged.

articles.body: Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any other human-made object. | Photo: NASA / Hulton Archive / Getty Images After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, "very, very far." The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet - equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours. It's the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1's journey isn't over yet. It's been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. articles.title: 1 light-day from Earth! NASA's Voyager 1 probe hits huge milestone in interstellar space
articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has officially hit one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026.
articles.body: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is now one light-day from Earth — so far away that it takes signals a full 24 hours to reach the probe. Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, just a couple of weeks after Voyager 2 lifted off. But Voyager 1 launched on a faster trajectory than its twin and has just become the first spacecraft to ever reach one light-day away, which is equivalent to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), or the distance that one light particle travels in 24 hours. The milestone — which Voyager 1 hit today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) — shows the incredible ingenuity, technical ability and creativity from the teams at NASA that continue to innovate to keep this mission going nearly five decades later.
